summary: In Greek mythology, Taras (Ancient Greek Τάρας) was the eponymous hero of Taras (Tarentum, modern Taranto) in Magna Graecia. Son of Poseidon by the nymph Satyrion (or a daughter of Minos), he was saved from shipwreck by a dolphin his father sent; riding it from Taenarum to southern Italy, he founded the city and river that bear his name. Pausanias records his hero cult; Tarentine coins show the boy on a dolphin.
etymology: Taras names both the hero and the colonial city; the nearby harbour Torre Saturo preserves the Satyrion toponym of his mother's country.

sections.heading: Family and foundation
paragraphs: Taras is son of Poseidon and Satyrion — either a local Tarentine nymph or a Minoan princess. When he is shipwrecked, Poseidon sends a dolphin; Taras rides it across the sea from the Laconian promontory of Taenarum to Italy and founds Tarentum.

Pausanias treats him as the hero who named both city and river. Historical Spartan colonisation of the Iapygian site (traditionally late eighth century BC) overlays the mythic eponym; the first Spartan foothold is remembered near Satyrion/Torre Saturo.

sections.heading: Iconography
paragraphs: Silver coins of ancient Taras show the youth astride a dolphin, sometimes holding Poseidon's trident — the same image survives on modern Taranto's emblem. Kindred dolphin-riders in myth include Arion, Melicertes/Palaemon, and Apollo Delphinios, but Taras remains the local founder of the Italian colony.
The atlas id taras-hero is this Poseidon-son. He is not Taras the river alone, nor a Roman historical founder.
